'''Film Ventures International''' ('''FVI''') was an independent film production and distribution company originally located in [[Atlanta, Georgia]], during the 1970s. FVI garnered a notorious reputation within the industry for producing films that were highly derivative of many [[blockbuster (entertainment)|blockbusters]] of the era. The company mainly specialized in producing and distributing [[B movie]]s and [[Horror film|horror]] fare.<ref name="badmovieplanet.com">{{cite web|title=The Unknown Movies, FVI: What You Didn't Know |work=badmovieplanet.com |url=http://www.badmovieplanet.com/unknownmovies/reviews/fvi.html |access-date=2007-06-25 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020418172705/http://www.badmovieplanet.com/unknownmovies/reviews/fvi.html |archive-date=2002-04-18 }}</ref>

== History ==
The entrepreneur who spearheaded the company was [[Edward L. Montoro]]. He wrote, directed, and produced the company's first feature film ''Getting Into Heaven'' in 1968. The [[adult film]] was made for $13,000 and grossed almost 20 times its cost.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Unknown Movies, Readers' FVI Questions |work=badmovieplanet.com |url=http://www.badmovieplanet.com/unknownmovies/reviews/fvi2.html |access-date=2007-06-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020612071757/http://www.badmovieplanet.com/unknownmovies/reviews/fvi2.html |archive-date=2002-06-12 }}</ref>

FVI was known for acquiring Italian genre films and distributing them within the United States. These films included the 1968 [[spaghetti Western]] ''[[Boot Hill (film)|Boot Hill]]'', a sequel to the famous ''[[They Call Me Trinity|Trinity]]'' films, and the 1974 horror thriller ''[[Beyond the Door (1974 film)|Beyond the Door]]'' starring [[Juliet Mills]].

FVI acquired ''Beyond the Door'' for $100,000 and the film went on to earn $9 million at the box office, making it one of the most successful independent releases of that year. Detailing a woman possessed by a demon, ''Beyond the Door'' was labeled a rip-off of ''[[The Exorcist (film)|The Exorcist]]''. [[Warner Bros.]] promptly filed a lawsuit, claiming copyright infringement. The lawsuit failed after it was determined Warner Bros. had no rights to key horror scenes depicted in ''The Exorcist''.

FVI produced and distributed ''[[Grizzly (film)|Grizzly]]'' in 1976, one of the first of the ''[[Jaws (film)|Jaws]]'' imitations.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1976/05/13/archives/william-girdlers-notquitesotoothsome-grizzly.html|title=William Girdler's Not-Quite-So-Toothsome 'Grizzly'|first=Vincent|last=Canby|work=The New York Times |date=May 13, 1976|via=NYTimes.com}}</ref> Montoro financed the film for $750,000 and it was directed by [[William Girdler]]. ''Grizzly'' was a surprise hit, earning more than $39 million and becoming the most financially successful independent film of 1976. Montoro decided to keep the profits for himself, resulting in a lawsuit against FVI by Girdler and producer/screenwriters Harvey Flaxman and David Sheldon. FVI eventually returned the profits to the filmmakers.<ref>{{cite web |title=William Girdler, Hollywood Films |work=williamgirdler.com |url=http://www.williamgirdler.com/hollywood.html |access-date=2007-06-25}}</ref> Montoro's FVI worked with Girdler on the animal horror thriller ''[[Day of the Animals]]'' the following year, though this collaboration did not achieve the success of ''Grizzly''.

Montoro eventually moved FVI's headquarters to Hollywood and began churning out multiple genre films over the next seven years, including ''Search and Destroy'' (1979) starring [[Don Stroud]], ''[[The Dark (1979 film)|The Dark]]'' (1979) starring [[William Devane]], ''[[The Visitor (1979 film)|The Visitor]]'' (1979) starring [[Glenn Ford]], ''[[H. G. Wells' The Shape of Things to Come]]'' (1979) starring [[Jack Palance]], ''[[Kill or Be Killed (1980 film)|Kill or Be Killed]]'' (1980), ''[[Kill and Kill Again]]'' (1981), the sequel to ''Kill or Be Killed'', ''[[The Incubus (1981 film)|The Incubus]]'' (1981) starring [[John Cassavetes]], ''[[Texas Lightning (film)|Texas Lightning]]'' (1981) starring [[Cameron Mitchell (actor)|Cameron Mitchell]], ''[[Pieces (film)|Pieces]]'' (1982) starring [[Christopher George]], ''[[They Call Me Bruce?]]'' (1982), ''[[The Pod People]]'' (1983), ''[[Vigilante (1982 film)|Vigilante]]'' (1983) starring [[Robert Forster]], ''[[The House on Sorority Row]]'' (1983), ''[[Mortuary (1983 American film)|Mortuary]]'' (1983) starring [[Bill Paxton]], ''[[The Power (1984 film)|The Power]]'' (1984), ''Alley Cat'' (1984), and ''[[Mutant (1984 film)|Mutant]]'' (1984) starring [[Bo Hopkins]].<ref name="badmovieplanet.com"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Film Ventures International |work=IMDb |url=https://www.imdb.com/company/co0007463/ |access-date=2007-06-25}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Edward L. Montoro |work=IMDb |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0600162/ |access-date=2007-06-25}}</ref>

== Demise ==
In 1980, FVI acquired the rights to the Italian film ''[[Great White (1981 film)|Great White]]'', a thinly veiled ''Jaws'' rip-off starring [[James Franciscus]] and [[Vic Morrow]]. Montoro and FVI spent over $4 million in advertising in the U.S., but [[Universal Pictures]] promptly filed a lawsuit, claiming that the film was too derivative of ''Jaws''. Universal won the lawsuit and ''Great White'' was pulled from the theaters after just one week of release. The failure of ''Great White'' was a major monetary loss for FVI.<ref name="badmovieplanet.com"/><ref>{{cite web |title=IMDb, ''Ultimo squalo, L' '' (''Great White'') |work=IMDb |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0081677/ |access-date=2007-06-25}}</ref>

By 1984, FVI was on the verge of collapse due to multiple financial issues, including the release failure of ''Great White'', the poor box-office performance of the studio's final film ''Mutant'', and a pending divorce settlement of Montoro's. Surprising many within the industry, Montoro took $1 million from FVI and vanished, never to be seen again. Film Ventures International officially closed its doors in 1985, filing [[Chapter 11 bankruptcy]], and later being purchased by the INI Entertainment Group. Montoro's whereabouts remain unknown to this day, though it is believed he fled to Mexico.<ref name="badmovieplanet.com"/>

In 1987, Film Ventures International attempted to return to film production with a co-venture of April Films to set up a film project called ''The Prank'', and received a three-picture co-production deal over the next 12 months and with the acquisition of co-production and distribution of other ventures, after becoming a subsidiary of INI Entertainment Group (at that time it was called Independent Network Inc.).<ref>{{Cite news|last=Klein|first=Richard|date=1987-03-11|title=Film Ventures Intl. Back On the Beat With Coprod Deal|pages=15, 115|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref> That year, Film Ventures International acquired the rights to two feature films, namely ''Operation: Take No Prisoners'' and ''Phantom Empire'', two of the action films that were churned out for a ten-picture acquisition and in-house production blueprint for the next twelve months, slated to go through 1988.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1987-10-14 |title=Film Ventures Intl. Takes Two Indie Pix |page=6 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref>

== In other media ==
Some of their films, including fan favorites ''[[Extra Terrestrial Visitors|Pod People]]'' and ''[[Ator 2 – L'invincibile Orion|Cave Dwellers]]'', were eventually riffed by the cult TV series ''[[Mystery Science Theater 3000]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.flavorwire.com/603308/our-10-favorite-mystery-science-theater-3000-episodes|title=Our 10 Favorite 'Mystery Science Theater 3000' Episodes|first=Jason|last=Bailey|website=Flavorwire|date=12 April 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wrightonfilm.com/2009/08/01/keep-circulating-the-tapes-the-best-of-mst3k/|title=Keep Circulating the Tapes — The Best of MST3K|first=Benjamin|last=Wright|date=August 1, 2009}}</ref><ref name="filmventures">[https://www.pastemagazine.com/movies/film-ventures-international/from-grizzly-to-great-white-the-death-of-film-vent/ From Grizzly to Great White: The Death of Film Ventures International - Paste]</ref>
